job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much of a story, I'm afraid. I live with my parents in Little Marsh, a village forty minutes from the nearest town with any firms. Mornings I help my father, who's an electrician, on small jobs, rewiring a kitchen or fitting sockets. He pays me in lunch and a bit of fuel money. Afternoons I send applications by post and email, and on Sundays I go to church and sit with the older men afterwards, who ask if I've found anything yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what has the search been like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electronic and electrical engineering, finished in June with a good result. My final project was a motor controller for a small conveyor, and I spent ten weeks at a firm that makes control panels. They liked my work but said there's no budget for another hire. I've sent about fifty applications, had two interviews. I owe a lot in student loans and I've got maybe ten days of living costs in my account. My parents have given what they could, and now there's nothing left to give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how I always thought it would go. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and mostly it's a better tool. I'd tell the men at church that good work and a steady trade still count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be stuck. My problem isn't AI, my problem is that there are very few jobs near the village and companies prefer experienced people. I'd be doing the same thing, sending letters and waiting. With the loan on top, it's an unhappy position, but I don't think the world owes me anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with my father and take any small electrical jobs that come up, so I'd have a trade to point to. I'd apply at the control panel firm again every three months, so they remember me, and I'd look at an electrical apprenticeship scheme to get my qualifications recognised for site work. I'd also widen my search to towns further away and be ready to move if a firm offers a real position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. A steady sort of worry in the background, like the sound of the fridge. I try not to talk about it at home, because my parents carry enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want an employer to see in you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reliable worker who turns up on time and finishes what he starts. That's what my father says matters. He's been in the trade thirty years and he says clients remember who showed up and who didn't. The degree gets me through the door, and the character keeps me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about the help that's on offer for graduates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want handouts, and I'd say so. I'd rather have a job and earn my money. But it would help if the government made it cheaper for small firms to take on a young engineer. That's different from a handout, it's an opening. And I'd be grateful for the right to start my loan repayments only when I'm earning.

say: I'd tell the men at church that good work and a **steady** trade still count.
Every few years there's a new thing that changes everything, and mostly it's a better tool.
think: My problem isn't AI but few **local** jobs and firms that prefer experience.
The loan is heavy, but I don't think the world owes me anything.
do: Keep taking small electrical jobs with my **father** so I have a trade to point to.
Re-apply to the control panel firm every three months.
Look into an electrical apprenticeship and be ready to move for a real position.
feel: **Quiet** worry, like the sound of a fridge.
I hide it at home so my parents don't carry more.
S0.quote: The degree gets me through the door, and the character keeps me there.
fieldNote: He wants **work**, not help, and frames subsidies for small firms as an opening, not a handout.
His father is both employer and example, and the trade is his **fallback**.
He keeps worry private, so the family does not see its **size**.

steps.text: Take small electrical jobs with my father for fuel money
Re-apply to the control panel firm every three months
Enrol on an electrical apprenticeship scheme for site qualifications
Cut out all travel except to interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not something to be afraid of but it's something to respect. Firms that train people properly will come out of it fine, and firms that cut corners won't. I'd say the answer is apprenticeships and real work, not courses for their own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. At the control panel firm, a lot of my ten weeks was drawing wiring diagrams, checking parts lists and writing test sheets, and a program can already do much of that. If those jobs go, the firm needs fewer juniors. But the electrical work in a house, a factory or a farm still needs hands, and I can do that. That's why my father's trade seems safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder on the practical side, getting my qualifications for fitting and testing, and I'd go after jobs in maintenance, site installation and servicing. I'd keep away from jobs that are mostly screen work. I'd still not use AI myself, but if a firm told me to, I'd learn what they need. I'd do it quietly and not make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the feeling that the ground is shifting under the part of the job I studied for, while the part I learned from my father is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your control panel internship could software do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawings and the lists, mostly. In the panel shop there was a man called Gerd who'd done the paperwork for years, and I could see it was something a program could take over. The wiring, the testing, the fixing when something trips, that's still someone with a screwdriver and a meter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd ever use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. I've never touched one and don't feel I need to, but I'm not stupid. If the firm wants it, I'll learn it. I just don't want it doing my thinking for me, because I want to understand the thing I'm putting my name to.

say: I'd say it's something to **respect**, not fear, and firms that train properly will be fine.
The answer is apprenticeships and real work, not courses for their own sake.
think: Much of my internship was drawings and test sheets that programs can do, so firms need fewer **juniors**.
Electrical work with hands in a house, factory or farm feels safer.
do: Lean into the **practical** side: fitting, testing and maintenance jobs.
Avoid jobs that are mostly screen work.
Learn AI quietly only if a firm tells me to.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ground is shifting under the part I studied.

S1.quote: The wiring, the testing, the fixing when something trips, that's still someone with a screwdriver and a meter.
fieldNote: He splits his skills into **paper** and **hands**, and puts his hope in hands.

steps.text: Apply for maintenance, installation and servicing jobs
Qualify in fitting and testing through an apprenticeship scheme
Learn the AI tools a firm asks for, if hired

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and nobody has a plan, which is a scandal. I'd say that to the vicar, to the council and to anyone who'd listen. But I'd be honest that I don't think anyone has the answer, and I'd be uneasy about big promises from politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened, and I find it hard to say out loud. Two years isn't enough for a young man with a loan to get on his feet. I'd still be the beginner when software does all the paper work and the design. Even my father would feel it, as the quotes, the ordering and the scheduling go first. I don't know how we'd keep paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do everything I can to stay useful with my hands. I'd work with my father full time for nothing but my keep, and I'd get my electrical certificates so I can be on a site legally. I'd stop all spending except for fuel and food. I'd ask the church if there's any small work available. And I'd pray, honestly. I'm not ashamed of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like when you hear bad news in the night and can't tell anyone. I'd lie awake and run the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit up late in the kitchen, with a cup of tea and the radio off, and I'd say the loan out loud to my father. He'd be silent, and then he'd say we'll manage, and I wouldn't believe him, and he wouldn't believe himself. But we'd say it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd turn to for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, Pastor Hollis from the church, and an old teacher, Mr Brandt. Not the government. I'd talk to them over the garden fence. I'd ask them what they'd do in my place, and I'd weigh it up myself. I don't trust big promises from people who've never held a spanner.

say: I'd tell the vicar and the council that nobody has a plan, which is a **scandal**.
I'd stay wary of big promises from politicians.
think: Two years isn't enough for a young man with a loan, and my father's **quotes** and scheduling would go first too.
I don't know how we'd keep paying the mortgage.

feel: **Sick**, like bad news in the night that I can't share.
S2.quote: I don't trust big promises from people who've never held a spanner.
fieldNote: His panic is **private**, carried alone and shared only with his father in the kitchen.
Faith and village advisers matter more than **government**.

steps.text: Work for my father full time for my keep

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get your house in order, and I'd tell the lads to do just that. Learn a trade, save money, don't rely on the system. I'd also tell the council that if they want young people to stay in villages, they need to help them get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's less frightening but I'd still be nervous. With five years I could get a job, build up my certificates, maybe get a small business going with my father. By the time AGI lands I'd have some experience and savings, and the electrical trade is about three years behind. That's a decent head start, if I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my certificates in the first year and work with my father at the same time. I'd apply to the control panel firm and to three maintenance companies. I'd save a third of everything and pay down the smallest part of the loan first. By year three I'd see if my father and I can take on small commercial jobs. I'd also look at whether solar installation would suit us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better. It's like seeing the end of a long tunnel. There's something at the end, and I think I can reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't like it, but I'd go if the job was real. I'd want to be home for Sundays and for harvest time, and I'd miss my father's workshop. I'd go for two years at the most, and then see if I could come back and start our own firm. I'm not a drifter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about leaving the village for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big difference is time to build something that lasts. In two years there's no time. In five I can finish my qualifications and start a business. I'm a patient man and I like things that take time.

say: I'd tell the lads to **learn** a trade, save money and not rely on the system.
The council should help young people get started if they want them to stay in villages.
think: It's less frightening, and the electrical trade is about three years behind, a decent **head start**.

S3.quote: I'm a patient man and I like things that take time.
fieldNote: His plan is rooted in **family** and place: a small business with his father.
He would leave the village for two years at most and wants to come **back**.
Alarm remains because he expects juniors, including himself, to be cut.

steps.text: Finish electrical certificates in the first year
Apply to the control panel firm and three maintenance companies
Save a third of all earnings toward the loan
Explore solar installation work with my father

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and we shouldn't waste it worrying. I'd tell people at church that this is the time to build trades, families and communities that can hold up if things change. I'd say let the engineers and the firms do their work, and let us do ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite settled. Ten years is a whole working life's first chapter. I could get my qualifications, work, save, and by 2036 have a business or a steady job with a good name behind me. And the hands-on part of my trade stays safe a bit longer. I'd still worry about the loan and the economy, but not about my future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work with my father for a year or two, get my certificates, and set up a small firm with him doing domestic and small commercial electrical work. I'd pay the loan off by thirty, and I'd think about getting married and buying a small house in the village. I'd still not use AI unless I had to, but I'd learn the software that firms use for quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. There's a worry, but it's the ordinary kind. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you build a business with your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. He's fifty-eight and he'll want to hand it on to somebody. I'd bring in the books and the quotes side, and he'd keep the work. A father-and-son firm has a good ring to it, and clients like that. I'd rather be part of that than stuck on a screen in somebody's office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger lads in the village?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them a trade is not second best. You can have a degree and a trade, and a bit of both is the best protection. And honour your word, because people remember who kept it. Those things hold up in any year.

say: I'd tell people at church to build **trades**, families and communities that can hold up.
Let the engineers do their work, and let us do ours.
think: I'm quite **settled**: ten years is the first chapter of a working life.
The hands-on part of my trade stays safe a bit longer.

S4.quote: A trade is not second best. You can have a degree and a trade, and a bit of both is the best protection.
fieldNote: With ten years his outlook turns to **family**, home and a father-and-son business.
His father, fifty-eight, wants to hand the work on, which makes the **plan** natural.
He is less anxious here, but still carries the **loan** and expects ordinary pressures.

steps.text: Set up a small electrical firm with my father
Pay the student loan off by thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is no time to build a trade, pay a loan and get on your feet. What would help isn't a handout. It's apprenticeships, small firms being paid to take on young people, and loan payments that start only once I'm earning. And honest talk from leaders who don't make promises they can't keep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for much. We want a fair chance to work, to pay our way and to look after our families. I'd say too many people think a degree means a job, and it doesn't. I'd like the next lot of lads to know what I've learned, that you'd best have a trade in your hands as well.

headlineQuote: We want a fair chance to work, to pay our way and to look after our families.
portrait: Felix is a **23-year-old** electronic engineering graduate living with his parents in a village, with fifty applications, two interviews and no offer.
His electrician father is his employer and example, and he carries heavy debt with about **ten days** of costs saved.
He leans traditional and free-market, prefers work and apprenticeships to handouts, and draws advice from church and family.
Resistant to new technology, he never uses AI and puts his hope in **hands-on** electrical work.
He is anxious to panicked as warning shrinks, and uneasy only when ten years allows a father-and-son firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because two years is no time to build a trade or pay the loan.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships**, pay for small firms to hire young people, and loan payments that begin once he is earning.
